Q: Merging the headers then concatenate the records of a huge number of text files A:

Regarding the second problem - Argument list too long is a shell error message, not an awk one, and the usual solution is to have awk read the list of files from the input rather than passing them as arguments, e.g. using the builtin version of printf as it can't have that argument list size problem:

printf '%s\n' input*.vcf |
awk '
    BEGIN {
        while ( (getline file < ARGV[1]) > 0 ) {
            ARGV[ARGC++] = file
        }
    }
    ...
' -

If your input looks like this:

$ head input*.vcf
==> input1.vcf <==
##fileformat=VCFv4.2
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
chrom1 ...
chrom2 ...
...

==> input2.vcf <==
##fileformat=foo
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
this ...
that ...
...

then maybe something like this is what you're looking for, using any awk:

$ cat tst.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash

awk '
    BEGIN {
        while ( (getline file < ARGV[1]) > 0 ) {
            ARGV[ARGC++] = file
        }
        ARGV[1] = "pass=1"
        numFiles = ARGC-1
        ARGV[ARGC++] = "pass=2"
        for ( i=2; i<=numFiles; i++ ) {
            ARGV[ARGC++] = ARGV[i]
        }
    }
    FNR == 1  { endOfHdrs = 0 }
    (pass == 1) && !endOfHdrs
    (pass == 2) && endOfHdrs
    /^#CHROM/ { endOfHdrs = 1 }
' <(printf '%s\n' input*.vcf)


$ ./tst.sh
##fileformat=VCFv4.2
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
##fileformat=foo
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
chrom1 ...
chrom2 ...
...
this ...
that ...
...

Change ^#CHROM/ { endOfHdrs = 1 } to ^#CHROM/ { endOfHdrs = 1; if (pass==1) nextfile } or similar if necessary for improved performance.

Having said that, if all of the lines that start with # are headers then you could of course just do a couple of greps:

$ printf '%s\n' input*.vcf | xargs grep -h '^#'; printf '%s\n' input*.vcf | xargs grep -vh '^#'
##fileformat=VCFv4.2
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
##fileformat=foo
##contig=...
##INFO=...
##FORMAT=...
##...
#CHROM ...
chrom1 ...
chrom2 ...
...
this ...
that ...
...

Q: How can I connect to MongoDB running in a Docker container? A:

The problem was not related to Docker, but to the bindip in the configuration of MongoDB. See e.g., mongodb.conf bind_ip = 127.0.0.1 does not work but 0.0.0.0 works

Q: How can I create a database for a MongoDB container on startup? A:

There isn’t any need to create a database in advance (they're created on the fly), but it makes sense to create a non-root user the first time the container starts.

File docker-compose.yml

services:
  ...
  mongo:
    image: mongo:6-jammy
    env_file: [.env-mongo, .env]
    volumes:
      - mongo:/data/db
      - ./init-mongo.js:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init-mongo.js
      # - ./init-mongo.sh:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init-mongo.sh  # mongo < 6

volumes:
  mongo:

File init-mongo.sh doesn't need to be executable. It's sourced.

File .env (the application's variables)

MONGO_USER=user
MONGO_PASSWORD=userpasswd
MONGO_DB=foo

File .env-mongo (MongoDB service's variables):

MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME=root
MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD=rootpasswd
MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE=foo  # for mongo >= 6

Since mongo-6 one can use file process.env, it uses init-mongo.js. Before that, use init-mongo.sh (change the script that you attach in file docker-compose.yml, and MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE is not needed in this case).

File .env is meant to be used by the app service(s), and file .env-mongo by the mongo service.

MONGO_INITDB_* variables are used by the mongo's entry point_. The documentation can be found on Docker Hub. Also, it's the entrypoint that runs the initialization script.

File init-mongo.js

db.getSiblingDB('admin').auth(
    process.env.MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME,
    process.env.MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD
);
db.createUser({
    user: process.env.MONGO_USER,
    pwd: process.env.MONGO_PASSWORD,
    roles: ["readWrite"],
});

File init-mongo.sh

q_MONGO_USER=`jq --arg v "$MONGO_USER" -n '$v'`
q_MONGO_PASSWORD=`jq --arg v "$MONGO_PASSWORD" -n '$v'`
mongo -u "$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME" -p "$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD" admin <<EOF
    use foo;
    db.createUser({
        user: $q_MONGO_USER,
        pwd: $q_MONGO_PASSWORD,
        roles: ["readWrite"],
    });
EOF

More files are in a gist.

Q: Unable to connect to MongoDB running in a Docker container A:

I was using port 27017 instead of 49155 (doh, port forwarding)

0.0.0.0:49155->27017/tcp

Thanks to the ZeissS.

Q: Python class, attribute A:

As he explained, Python allows adding attributes to instances unless you explicitly prevent it. The additional detail here is that __c is name-mangled: inside the class it becomes _Esempio__c. When you assign ex1.__c = 'querty', you are creating a new attribute named __c, not modifying the original one. Since instance attributes are dynamic by default, no exception is raised.
